newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka decides not to increase tea imports.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka decides not to increase tea imports.

text.p: Sri Lanka has decided against letting in higher imports of tea for blending, fearing it could hurt prices at the world's biggest auction centre, government officials said on Monday.
"We will maintain the status quo...we're not expanding imports," a Plantation Industries Ministry official said.

Sections of the tea trade had asked the government to allow imports of main grade orthodox teas for a limited trial period with the long-term aim of making Colombo a blending centre like London and Rotterdam.

The Indian Ocean island, the world's second largest tea exporter, now allows imports of a limited quantity of CTC (cut, twist, curl) tea and specialty teas like Darjeelings for blending, packeting and re-export.
Only about two million kg of tea a year is currently imported. About four or five million kg of tea are sold each week at the Colombo auction, the world's largest.
Sri Lanka has about 18-20 percent market share and exported a record 244 million kg last year, up from 240 million kg in 1995.
"Opponents of the proposed (imports) scheme said that if we allow more imports it could depress auction prices and damage the image of Ceylon tea," a Tea Board official said.
Industry officials and analysts have said Sri Lankan tea prices are expected to remain strong this year, although off last year's record highs.

Tea prices soared late last year, mainly on strong winter demand for the distinctive low grown teas from the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), Sri Lanka's biggest tea market, and the Middle East.
The Colombo auction average price for calendar 1996 rose to 103.88 rupees ($1.76) per kg from the previous year's high of 72.21 rupees.
Sudath Munasinghe, director, tea, at brokers John Keells, said the trade had suggested expanding tea imports to improve packing and value-added production in the country.
"Some buyers are opening outlets abroad like in Dubai, Singapore and the Eastern bloc states," he said. "So most tea is going to go in bulk form and all their packeting will be done there.

"As a result, we could lose out on value-addition," he said. "Also, a large number of people are employed in packing tea, which is a very labour-intensive operation. If some exporters decide to do packing outside, our guys could lose jobs."
Munasinghe said some markets felt that the prices of Ceylon tea were too high and that the island could lose market share.
Sri Lanka had lost traditional markets such as Britain after heavy buying by Russia, the world's biggest tea importer, sent Ceylon tea prices soaring.
Tea brokers in London say Sri Lankan tea has almost priced itself out of a growing British market, with the daily "cuppa" now more likely to be an African blend such as Kenyan.
The British fondness for quick-brewing tea bags, which are less suited to the large-leaf teas produced in Sri Lanka, has also hit Ceylon tea imports.
